pages.x: To pay for the new St Peter's in Rome, the Church sold indulgences, papers said to shorten the time a soul spent being punished after death. One preacher, Johann Tetzel, was said to promise that as soon as a coin rang in the box, a soul sprang out of purgatory.

On 31 October 1517 Martin Luther, a monk and professor at Wittenberg, sent the archbishop 95 arguments against indulgences and, the story goes, nailed them to a church door. Printed copies spread across Germany within weeks.

Luther went further: people were saved by faith alone, he said, and the Bible, not the pope, was the final word. Cast out by the pope, he was called before the emperor Charles V at Worms in 1521 and refused to take back his words. He is said to have ended: here I stand, I can do no other.
Hidden in Wartburg castle by a friendly prince, Luther translated the New Testament from Greek into German in eleven weeks.
pages.fx: Ordinary people could now read the Bible for themselves, and his German became the base of the modern written language.

pages.x: Peasants took Luther's words as a call for freedom and rose across Germany in 1524 and 1525. Luther urged the princes to crush them, and they did.

Others went their own way: Zwingli in Zurich, John Calvin in Geneva, and the Anabaptists, who baptised only adults. In England, Henry VIII broke with Rome in 1534, less over faith than because the pope would not end his marriage, and made himself head of the Church of England.

After years of war, the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 let each German prince choose whether his land would be Catholic or Lutheran, and his subjects had to follow or move. The Catholic Church answered with reforms of its own at the Council of Trent.

The Reformation split Western Christianity into Catholic and Protestant churches. It led to a century of religious wars, but also spread reading and schooling and new ideas about conscience. Today some 800 million people are Protestants.
